title: The words of return
hook: Adam receives words from his Lord and turns back, and is forgiven (2:37; 7:23)

segments.voice: Yesterday: waswas, the whisper that renamed the tree. Your line was not every voice is yours. Did you let one whisper pass? Day twenty-seven.

Think of the last time you really messed up, and knew it. The stomach drop. And then the fork in the road. One way: explain. It wasn't really my fault. They pushed me. Anyone would have. The other way: three hard words. I was wrong. Most of us know which one is easier in the moment, and which one actually lets you breathe again afterward. Yesterday, Adam and his wife ate from the one tree, and their shame appeared. They're standing in the garden, covering themselves with leaves. This is their fork in the road. And the story remembers someone else who stood at one too.
screen: `THE STOMACH DROP.` → `EXPLAIN IT, OR SAY I WAS WRONG.` → `ADAM'S FORK IN THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Remember Iblis. When he refused to bow, and was sent out, whose fault did he say it was? In surah seven, he says to God: because You have sent me astray. He blamed God. Now listen to Adam and his wife, in the same surah, in Pickthall's words: “Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If thou forgive us not and have not mercy on us, surely we are of the lost!” We have wronged ourselves. No excuse. No blaming the whisperer, or each other. And surah two tells what happened next: “Then Adam received from his Lord words (of revelation), and He relented toward him.” Many commentators say those words were this very prayer. God gave Adam the words to come back with. The word for it is tawbah, and its root, t-w-b, means to turn back, to return. Here's the beautiful part. The same root is used for God. One of His names is at-Tawwab: the One who keeps turning back toward the one who turns. The verse ends: “Lo! He is the Relenting, the Merciful.” So tawbah isn't groveling. It's two turns: you turn around, and you find you're being turned toward. A hadith in Bukhari and Muslim pictures it. A man loses his camel in the desert, with all his food and water on it, and lies down to die. He wakes, and it's standing there. God, the hadith says, is happier with a servant's tawbah than that man is with his camel. And Muslims draw one more thing from this: Adam was forgiven, there and then. The story of humanity, in Islam, starts with a mistake, and a return that worked.
screen: `IBLIS BLAMED GOD.` · `WE HAVE WRONGED OURSELVES.` · `TAWBAH — TO TURN BACK.` · `AT-TAWWAB — THE ONE WHO TURNS TOWARD.` · then, large: `HE RELENTED TOWARD HIM.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you two minutes. Let one thing come to mind that you're sorry for. Not the biggest thing in your life. Just something real, from this week or this year. Notice if an excuse comes up with it. Set the excuse down. Then, if you pray, say sorry to God, in your own words, as plainly as Adam did. If you don't pray, say it silently to the person you let down, or just to yourself: I was wrong. Then sit, and notice what it feels like to have turned around. The bell holds the time.
Tawbah. Turning back, repentance: you turn toward God, and find God turning toward you. At-Tawwab.
Your line: we wronged ourselves; forgive us. Today, the next time you're wrong about something, even something tiny, skip the explanation and just say so. Day twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims make tawbah by stopping the wrong, regretting it, resolving not to return to it, and, where someone was harmed, putting it right; many recite Adam's words from 7:23 in their prayers.

fork.reveal: "Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves." and God relented toward him. Iblis, at his fork, had blamed God.

original.note: Arabic: repentance, turning back, from t-w-b, to return; God's name at-Tawwab shares the root.

trapdoor: what you thought: repentance means feeling terrible about yourself.
what it means: tawbah — turning back to God, without excuses, and being turned toward in return.

what a scholar hears: t-w-b is used both of the servant (taba ila) and of God (taba 'ala); many commentators say the words Adam received in 2:37 are the prayer of 7:23; and Muslims read the story as forgiveness complete, with nothing inherited.

notes: Pickthall 7:23 and 2:37 quoted from memory; confirm exact wording.
That the 'words' of 2:37 are the prayer of 7:23: the view of many early commentators (e.g. reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid); other views exist. Stated as 'many commentators say'.
Iblis in 7:16 ('Now, because Thou hast sent me astray...'): paraphrased. Confirm.

'Nothing inherited': Muslims hold that Adam's sin was forgiven and no one bears another's burden (6:164). The script says 'Muslims draw one more thing from this' and does not mention or compare with other traditions. Confirm tone.
Conditions of tawbah in howItsDone (stop, regret, resolve, restore rights): the common scholarly list (e.g. al-Nawawi). Confirm.
Practice: 'say sorry to God in your own words' follows the outline; no prayer text is written for the listener.
